claim: An independent vendor source corroborates the TikTok payout-rate discontinuity: the legacy Creator Fund paid roughly $0.01-$0.04 per 1,000 views while the successor Creator Rewards Program pays roughly $0.40-$1.00+ per 1,000 views, a 10-40x change that makes TikTok per-view earnings non-comparable across the 2023-2024 program boundary.
stance_target: The claim that platform monetization scheme changes break longitudinal comparability of creator income figures
scope_conditions: Murf.ai (an AI voiceover vendor) content-marketing blog, last updated 16 March 2026, originally published 21 September 2022; rates described as what creators 'commonly report' and 'most creators reported' — self-reported, no sample size, no survey, no country breakdown; corroborates the same bands published by unrelated aggregators, so the structural shift is robust even though the precise figures are not
quoted_support: Today, eligible creators commonly report earning $0.40 to $1.00+ per 1,000 views under the program. This is a huge jump from payouts under the original TikTok Creator Fund, which hovered in the $0.02 to $0.04 range.

claim: TikTok's Creator Rewards Program is explicitly country-gated — eligibility requires being 'in a supported country (TikTok defines where the program is active)' — so platform-native monetization is unavailable to creators in unsupported markets regardless of audience size.
stance_target: The claim that US/Western creator-income findings do not generalize to Southeast Asia because monetization access itself is geographically unequal
scope_conditions: Eligibility list as stated in March 2026; the supported-country list is not enumerated on the page, so which SEA markets are covered cannot be determined from this source; the age requirement is 18, or 19 in South Korea, indicating jurisdiction-specific variation in the program's terms
quoted_support: A personal account (business accounts, political or government accounts are excluded) Be at least 18 years old (19 in South Korea) Be in a supported country (TikTok defines where the program is active) Have at least 10,000 followers Accumulate 100,000 video views in the past 30 days

claim: TikTok monetization eligibility imposes a compound floor — 10,000 followers, 100,000 qualified views in the past 30 days, and a one-minute minimum video length — meaning any earnings distribution measured over monetized TikTok creators is a severely truncated sample that excludes the entire population of small and short-form creators.
stance_target: The claim that reported creator income distributions systematically exclude the unmonetized majority and therefore overstate typical earnings
scope_conditions: Only 'qualified' views count — views from the For You feed meeting engagement thresholds, excluding short skips, paid promotions and content flagged low quality — so the effective view bar is higher than the nominal 100,000; account must also be in good standing with no serious violations
quoted_support: It's worth noting that views must be "qualified," views counted from the For You feed, not short skips, not paid promotions, and not flagged as low quality. Basically, you can't just "turn on monetization."

claim: TikTok creator payout rates vary systematically by audience geography, with viewers from the US, UK, Canada and Australia commanding higher RPMs than other markets — a structural mechanism by which identical audience size yields materially different income outside Western markets.
stance_target: The claim that Western creator-income benchmarks cannot be transferred to Southeast Asian creators
scope_conditions: Asserted without quantification — no RPM figures by country, no sample, no data source; the page's commercial purpose is selling AI dubbing to help creators reach higher-RPM markets, a direct conflict of interest in emphasising the geographic RPM gap
quoted_support: Audience location plays a major role in ad value, with viewers from the U.S., UK, Canada, and Australia typically bringing in higher RPMs. The age group and purchasing power of your followers also affect how much does TikTok pay for views, since advertisers pay more to target high-value markets.
numbers: no RPM figures given by country

claim: The TikTok Creator Fund's fixed-pool design mechanically diluted per-creator payouts as participation grew — a static pool distributed among all eligible creators regardless of how many joined — which explains why per-view rates fell and why creators reported no correlation between views and earnings.
stance_target: The claim that early platform creator funds structurally could not scale to support creator incomes
scope_conditions: Mechanism description, not measurement; no data on pool size over time or participant counts; consistent with the fund's documented replacement but offered without supporting figures
quoted_support: The Creator Fund program operated on a static pool of money that was distributed among all eligible creators, regardless of the number of creators who joined. As a result, payouts were inconsistent and quite low.

claim: Dissatisfaction with Creator Fund payout levels and opacity is documented as driving creators to abandon the program — 'this led many creators to diversify their monetization strategies or leave the fund altogether' — but no source in the vendor layer quantifies how many left.
stance_target: The claim that documented reasons for creator attrition are accompanied by measured quit rates
scope_conditions: Qualitative assertion with no survey, no sample size, no attrition rate; reasons given are low payouts, lack of transparency, no clear correlation between view count and earnings, and no reward for longer-form content; describes leaving a monetization program, not leaving content creation
quoted_support: Payouts lacked transparency, content performance wasn't always rewarded fairly, and there was no clear correlation between view count and earnings. ... This led many creators to diversify their monetization strategies or leave the fund altogether.
